**Lithium-ion batteries themselves.** A lithium-ion cathode needs lithium by definition, because lithium ions carry the charge. rendered:
Yes. The sodium battery papers in this collection show batteries whose cathodes, and the ions they carry, contain no lithium. Most of the other papers look at a different problem: removing cobalt from lithium-ion cathodes, not lithium.

**1. A sodium–sulfur battery that runs at room temperature.** The cathode is sulfur held inside the tiny pores of carbon made from table sugar. The authors describe a microporous confinement cathode for a room-temperature sodium sulfur battery[1]. It delivers a reversible capacity over 700 mAh/gS at 0.1C rates[2] and shows retention of over 300 mAh/gS capacity across 1500 cycles[3]. The authors stress that it is built from table sugar, sulfur, and sodium, all of which are cheap and earth abundant[4]. They also list the drawbacks of sodium–sulfur compared with lithium–sulfur: greater volume expansion (260% for Na versus 80% for Li)[5], and low Coulombic efficiency caused by instability at both electrodes.

**2. A sodium battery with no anode and a pyrite (iron sulfide) cathode.** The authors employed pyrite (FeS2) for the cathode as it is a cheap, abundant material[6]. Pyrite contains no sodium of its own, so the authors added sodium to it before building the cell (they call this presodiating). This cell reaches energy densities of ∼400 Wh/kg[7]. The authors say that is far surpassing recent reports on SIBs and even the theoretical maximum for LIB technology (387 Wh/kg for LiCoO2/graphite cells)[8]. Some cautions: that energy density is calculated from the mass of the presodiated pyrite and the carbon layer only, and the paper shows its stability over 40 cycles[9]. The paper explains why sodium appeals: it is a cheaper, more sustainable alternative because of the 1000× greater natural abundance of sodium in comparison to lithium[10]. It also notes the downside: sodium-ion batteries usually give up some energy density.

**3. Other ions beyond sodium.** A paper on straining V2O5 electrodes suggests the same approach could help hosts store sodium and potassium ions, as well as multivalent ions (Mg^2+ and Ca^2+)[11]. It notes that the size of these ions remains a challenge, and that strain could help offset this, describing it as a possible important tool for moving beyond lithium[12]. That paper does not demonstrate a working cell with these ions; it only proposes the idea.

**Lithium-ion batteries themselves.** A lithium-ion cathode needs lithium by definition, because lithium ions carry the charge. The remaining papers are about cutting cobalt from these cathodes (for example, the nickel–iron–aluminum oxide cathodes described as new cobalt-free cathodes for lithium-ion batteries), about coatings, or about recycling. None of them covers lithium-free cathodes.

**Bottom line:** lithium-free cathodes are possible if you switch chemistry, mainly to sodium. In these papers sodium cells trade some performance for cheaper, more abundant materials. The authors present them mainly as candidates for low-cost grid storage, while also reporting the high energy density described above.
